Learned methods can guide searches through high-dimensional spaces, fit empirical patterns where no analytical model is available, and propose candidate structures a designer would not have drafted. Computer systems and chip design put those capabilities to a hard test. An architectural decision begins with high-level software intent and cascades through compilers, instruction set architectures, microarchitectures, and register-transfer level (RTL) netlists down to physical silicon signoff. Every observation along that path is expensive, noisy, and partial. Compilers, cycle-level simulators, formal verification engines, and post-layout timing tools each expose a narrow slice of system behavior, and their assumptions often conflict. In hardware, the cost of an error is also asymmetric. A timing glitch or coherence bug discovered after tapeout may require revised masks and another pass through fabrication if firmware changes or validated operating restrictions cannot contain it. Respins are not rare. In the 2024 Wilson Research Group study, only 14 percent of surveyed integrated-circuit projects achieved first-silicon success [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024].

That asymmetric penalty is both the danger and the opportunity of automated design. Generative models can draft candidate RTL and architectural variations far faster than physical toolchains can evaluate them, but proposing alternatives creates engineering value only when the system can qualify what they physically achieve. An *AI-native design system* rebuilds the exploration loop around the tools that return evidence. It connects learned surrogates, deterministic simulators, and physical signoff engines through machine-usable state representations, so that hardware and software trade-offs can be explored systematically under an explicit verification budget.

Pursuing that closed loop is what led Amir Yazdanbakhsh and me to formulate the Architecture 2.0 moonshot in our initial paper [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. The proposal met with candid skepticism across the computer architecture community. The hard part was carrying learned exploration across architectural boundaries, so that changes in hardware organization and software mapping could respond to physical feedback while the system's requirements still held.

That proposal builds on decades of automation in synthesis, verification, and design-space exploration. Learned optimization had also reached commercial implementation before our paper appeared: in February 2023, Synopsys reported that its customers had registered the first 100 commercial tape-outs made with DSO.ai, its reinforcement-learning optimizer for block-level implementation [@Synopsys2023DSOai]. Such results show learned optimization in use within the reported design flows. Extending exploration across subsystem boundaries is harder. It requires coordinating tool assumptions, revisiting hardware and software interfaces, and checking the consequences of those changes together.

This book aims beyond isolated point assistance and bounded subsystem optimization. The question is whether a complete, closed-loop design system can find better architectures, reduce the engineering cost of finding them, or do both. I wrote this book to make that possibility concrete without assuming its success. The chapters develop the principles, state representations, and execution harnesses the moonshot requires.

The architectural problem always comes first. Depending on the physical constraints, the right engineering choice may combine learned surrogates, heuristic optimization, formal proofs, or conventional analysis with no machine learning at all. Architecture 2.0 does not claim that every circuit needs an AI model. It is the discipline of building AI-native design systems and holding them to an architecture-grade evidence standard, and its first question is where AI earns its place and what physical evidence its recommendations must deliver.

## On the Title of This Book {.unnumbered}

Each term in the title, *Architecture 2.0: Principles of AI-Native System and Chip Design*, sets a boundary. Architecture 2.0 names two things the book keeps apart. The first is a proposed shift in how architecture work is done: extending established task and subsystem automation into coordinated, closed-loop exploration across the full hardware–software stack. The second is the discipline that shift demands, which is what the chapters teach. That discipline carries high-level system intent through closed-loop exploration to physically checked results and qualifies that evidence against strong non-learned baselines, while commitment authority stays with named people. The shift is a claim the book argues for, and the discipline is what lets a reader check it. *Principles* is in the title because model weights and tool scripts are transient, while the underlying physics, evidence standards, and architectural trade-offs outlast them.

*AI-native* means that the exploration workflow, represented state, and verification harnesses are organized around learned search that can revisit hardware–software choices across abstraction boundaries. *System and Chip Design* reflects the physical fact that a silicon floorplan cannot be optimized apart from the software workloads, compiler lowering passes, memory hierarchies, and thermal constraints that govern its behavior.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

The recurring case study is the Lighthouse study: a real-time mobile extended-reality (XR) compute subsystem specified for a strict 3\ W thermal design power budget and tight area limits. The study is prospective; it traces an architectural hypothesis through the evidence an engineering claim would require. The chapters frame its governing question around the 3\ W limit, build a machine-usable representation of its design state, and identify the methods and deterministic tool runs needed to evaluate candidates.

Judging whether an automated workflow improves a design program means examining the whole system of people and tools. A fluent generative model inside a broken verification loop only produces invalid silicon faster. A modest, well-calibrated surrogate that removes a weeks-long simulation bottleneck, on the other hand, can change a tapeout schedule. Every method in this book faces two questions. *Did the complete approach improve the architecture result, or reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable one, against a credible alternative?* And *should a named authority commit physical silicon to the result?* The first question is technical and measurable. The second is an organizational judgment that a person makes and owns.

Answering those questions means governing the whole exploration life cycle rather than a single point tool. The chapters teach three moves: formulating the question and representing the design state, connecting methods to real tools and qualifying what those tools return, and evaluating the complete approach and owning the commitment that follows. One team can make all three with the tools it already has. The book changes altitude once, at the end, to ask which of the limits such a team reaches are shared across the discipline rather than local to that team.

The Lighthouse study opens with intent formulation in @sec-moonshot, develops state representations in @sec-data-representations-world-models, and exposes incomplete execution prerequisites in @sec-architecture-20-ontology and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces. Its cache study stops before tool dispatch. A separate systolic-array study completes a pre-registered simulator comparison on synthetic matrix-multiplication kernels. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust examine those measured simulator returns, and @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack asks whether the local result transfers to another workload. Neither record establishes the Lighthouse subsystem's physical performance: its power envelope, accelerator, memory traffic, and thermal behavior still have to be evaluated together. Both records return in @sec-what-architect-owns, where the book applies its evidence standard to its own findings and states what remains necessary before commitment.

Architecture 2.0 sits at the intersection of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation (EDA; @fig-book-composition). Each overlap already has a field of work behind it. Architecture and machine learning help us predict performance and search large design spaces. Architecture and EDA connect system choices to RTL and physical implementation. Machine learning and EDA are already changing synthesis, placement, routing, and verification. What we are after sits where all three meet.

![**Architecture 2.0 unifies computer architecture, machine learning, and EDA.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design trade-offs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with physical evidence or estimates. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="100%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection."}

Work at that intersection has to satisfy all three fields at once. A generated artifact that ignores the workload is not an architecture result. A promising estimate that cannot survive implementation is not a physical result. A successful tool run without a fair comparison does not show that AI improved the work.

The scope of automation matters when judging such claims. Helping with one task, optimizing a subsystem within fixed interfaces, and searching across system boundaries demand different capabilities and checks. @sec-moonshot develops this distinction through three operational layers; the moonshot pursues the broadest scope all the way to physically verified silicon. This book is not a catalog of neural architectures, a prompt-engineering recipe, or a defense of unconstrained automation. Nor does it argue that heuristics should replace architectural judgment or formal verification. Physical signoff checks remain decisive, and named human architects remain accountable for every committed tapeout.

## The Discipline of Design Principles {.unnumbered}

Machine-learning models, EDA scripts, and the prompts and wrappers written around them go stale within months. What lasts is a principle rooted in semiconductor physics, the cost of a measurement, and documented failures. A true architectural principle will still govern the silicon outcome even if model capability grows by orders of magnitude and inference cost falls to zero. A team that grounds its automated design work in problem formulation, explicit state representation, tool discipline, adversarial evaluation, and human commitment authority can adopt each new model without rebuilding its method.

Each principle appears alongside the technical problem that calls for it. Most chapters state one or two in design-principle callouts that pair the principle with how to apply it. The companion @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes gathers the borrowed laws and paradoxes the chapters invoke, from Amdahl's law to the optimizer's curse, as a quick reference for derivations.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the practicing computer architect, chip designer, and systems researcher. The book assumes familiarity with performance, power, area, and hardware–software interfaces, along with working literacy in engineering software (Python, C++, or a standard hardware description language). No background in deep learning is required; the machine-learning ideas the argument needs are introduced where they are used, through concrete architecture problems and physical constraints.

Because Architecture 2.0 draws on fields that have mostly worked apart, the book is written for four technical communities:

- **Computer architects** who want to bring automated search and generative models into design exploration without loosening the physical checks that make a result trustworthy.
- **EDA and CAD engineers** looking to connect synthesis, placement, and verification toolchains to high-level architectural decision loops.
- **Machine learning and ML-systems researchers** entering hardware design who need to see how physical signoff, evaluation costs, and formal verification change what counts as a valid result.
- **Graduate students and engineering leaders** working across hardware and software who need a framework and a shared vocabulary for governing AI-native systems engineering.

## How to Read This Book {#book-structure .unnumbered}

The eleven chapters are cumulative and follow an architectural study from initial intent through evaluation to the decision whether to commit:

- @sec-moonshot, @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, and @sec-architecture-20-ontology set out the moonshot and its evidence standard, analyze the physical scaling limits and economic pressures straining manual design loops, and introduce the six-stage design life cycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), grounded in the running Lighthouse mobile XR study.
- @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, and @sec-feedback-verification-trust build the engineering infrastructure of Architecture 2.0: structured state representations, smallest sufficient methods, isolated tool harnesses, and the qualification of returned signals before they drive any action.
- @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, and @sec-what-architect-owns analyze cross-stack pattern transfer, apply adversarial red-teaming and matched-budget evaluation, and establish nondelegable human commitment authority.
- @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem charts the shared schemas, precompetitive open infrastructure, grand challenges, and university curricula needed to sustain an open research ecosystem.

Reading sequentially gives the complete engineering argument, and each of the four communities above can also enter through the chapters closest to its own work (@tbl-reading-paths). Three chapters form the spine every path shares: the moonshot and its evidence standard (@sec-moonshot), the life cycle that organizes the work (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), and the commitment decision that ends it (@sec-what-architect-owns).

| **Reader** | **Start with** | **Then** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Computer architect | @sec-moonshot, @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, @sec-architecture-20-ontology | @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-what-architect-owns |
| EDA and CAD engineer | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack |
| Machine learning researcher | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect |
| Graduate student or engineering leader | @sec-moonshot, @sec-architecture-20-ontology | @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, @sec-what-architect-owns, @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem |
: **Four reading paths through the same argument.** EDA developers and ML researchers gain most from the chapters on state representations and execution harnesses; architects and engineering leaders gain most from the chapters on transfer, evaluation, and ownership. Every path passes through the moonshot, the life cycle, and the commitment decision. {#tbl-reading-paths tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

The book's repository also carries four companion teaching labs for the systolic-array, RTL-timing, floorplan, and hardware–software examples. They are exercises for reasoning about design loops, not measurements. Where the tools are installed, the labs call SCALE-Sim, Yosys, Icarus Verilog, and a RISC-V compiler. Elsewhere they fall back to simplified analytical models, and several of their outcomes are set by hand rather than computed. None of them reaches physical signoff.

As you read, test these principles against a live design problem in your own work. Ask which decision matters, which hidden physical constraints must be exposed, which baseline comparison is fair, what the tools actually measured, and what risks remain unverified. The measure of this book is whether its principles carry to design problems it never mentions.

Artificial intelligence is likely to change how architects design chips and systems. Whether it does depends on the discipline taking that prospect seriously without taking anyone's claims on faith, this book's included. Generating code is not that change. The change, if it comes, will come from design systems that carry intent to checked physical results and from architects with the judgment to govern them.
